This is guarding the borders and corners
striving to create petty regulations.
The generals and ministers of Emperor Gēngshǐ 更始帝 were unable to defend,
and instead allowed petty figures to flourish.

See *Records of the Grand Historian: Biography of Qíng Bù* (集解), *Wen Xuan: Discourse on Board Games* (note), *The Long and Short Classic*, two sections on "National Power," *Imperial Readings of the Taiping Era* 753, and *Forest of Meanings*.
When Emperor Gēngshǐ 更始帝 arrived in Cháng'ān 長安,
his ministers' rejection of matters pertaining to the Eastern Palace
was ridiculed by those below.
They only built a small watchtower,
residing in half of the city.
From this, we can know that his generals and ministers were not of the same caliber as Xiāo Hé 蕭何 and Cáo Cāo 曹操.
See *Chū Xué Jì* 初學記, volume 24.
Now, words and deeds lie in being beautiful and good,
not in being numerous.
Utter one beautiful word, perform one beautiful deed,
and the world will follow it.
Or witness one evil thought, one ugly deed, and all the people will turn away from it.
Can one not be careful?
Therefore, the *Yì* 易 (Book of Changes) says:
"Words and deeds are the hinge of a gentleman,
the movement of the hinge
is the master of honor and disgrace,
and that by which heaven and earth are moved."
See *Qún Shū Zhì Yào* 群書治要.
Wáng Wēng 王翁 executed people,
and then added further poison and harm to them.
He even burned people alive,
and used five kinds of poison to pour into the muscles of the dead.
After burying them,
he covered them with thorns.
Once a person is dead,
they are equivalent to earth and wood;
even if you inflict more wounds and poison,
what harm or benefit is there?
Tāng Chéng Tāng 成湯's examination and acceptance [of requests],
did not benefit the officers and people;
the officers and people were drawn to him
He praised them for their virtuous benevolence.
Qí Xuān's 齊宣 act of sparing the ox,
Did no benefit to the wise,
The wise approved of it,
Because they valued his benevolent heart.
King Wén's 文王 burial of the dried bones,
Did no benefit to the common people,
The common people were pleased by it,
Because his kindness and righteousness moved people.
Wáng Wēng's 王翁 mutilation of the dead,
Observing people's five viscera,
Did no harm to the living,
The living hated it,
Because he showed it with cruelty.
These four matters,
Are negligible yet evident,
Minute yet still great.
Therefore, the two sages arose,
And one ruler was praised,
Wáng Wēng 王翁 perished,
Knowing the grand scheme and not knowing it are far apart!
See *Qún Shū Zhì Yào* 《群書治要》.
Sage kings governed the state,
Exalting ritual propriety and deference,
Promoting benevolence and righteousness,
Taking esteeming the worthy and cherishing the people as their task.
This is why divination and casting lots were few,
Sacrifices are for sparing use.
See *Qún Shū Zhì Yào*.
Formerly, King Líng of Chǔ was arrogant and extravagant, belittling his subordinates.
He disregarded the wise and devoted himself to spirits,
believing in the ways of shamans and oracles.
He fasted and purified himself, offering clean sacrifices
to worship the Supreme Deity (Shàngdì),
and to honor his assembled ministers.
He personally held the feathered staff,
dancing before the altar.
When the people of Wú came to attack,
his people urgently reported the crisis.
But King Líng continued drumming and dancing, as if nothing was happening.
He turned and replied,
"I am currently sacrificing to the Supreme Deity,
delighting the luminous spirits.
I shall surely receive blessings and aid from them,
and therefore cannot go to the rescue."
Consequently, the Wú troops arrived,
capturing his crown prince and concubines,
which is deeply lamentable.
See *Yù Lǎn*, 526, and 735.
Wáng Wēng was fond of divination and prognostication,
believing in auspicious times and days,
and was earnestly devoted to serving ghosts and spirits.
He built many temples and ancestral shrines,
purifying himself and offering sacrifices.
The expense of sacrificial offerings and delicacies,
and the hardship of the officials and soldiers in preparing them,
are not worth mentioning!
If the government is not good,
it will see the whole world betray it.
When disaster strikes and war breaks out,
it has no strategies to save itself.
Then it rushes to the southern suburbs to pray,
sincerely expressing its grievances,
wailing and weeping,
kowtowing and begging for its life,
hoping that Heaven will have pity and help it.
On the day the soldiers entered the palace,
arrows rained down,
and fires blazed up.
He fled under the Jiàntái Terrace,
still clutching his talismanic books and the Wēidǒu he had made.
One could say he was extremely deluded!
See *Qúnshū Zhìyào*.
*Jiànzhēng Dìwǔ*
Dōngfāng Shuò's short and superficial words
were considered trustworthy.
Everyone said that Shuò was highly intelligent,
and later sages could not match him.
The translation says:
"A rustic takes a fox for a civet cat,
Using the *sè* zither as a *kōnghóu* harp,
this is not merely failing to understand the difference between a fox and a *sè* zither,
but also failing to understand the difference between a wildcat and a *kōnghóu* harp.
This is not only speaking of the past,
but also failing to understand later worthies."
See *Yì Lín*; *Yì Wén Lèi Jù*, 44.
Previously, I was *Diǎn Yuè Dàfū* (Grand Master of Music),
a *xiāo* owl cried on the tree in the courtyard,
and everyone in the office was worried and fearful.
Later, I had a dispute with the *Diǎn Yuè* Xiè Hóu,
and we were both dismissed from our positions.
See *Yù Lǎn*, 496, also 927.
I was returning from Cháng'ān to Pèi,
and I fell ill on the way.
Covered with floss silk blankets
and a crimson
wool-lined short coat, riding a chestnut horse,
I stayed overnight in the eastern pavilion of a lower-level city.
The pavilion chief suspected I was a thief
and sent soldiers to attack at night.
I ordered the officers not to fight,
and after questioning each other, they dispersed and left.
This is about peacefully preserving oneself.
See *Běi Táng Shū Chāo*, 129; *Yì Wén Lèi Jù*, 75; *Yù Lǎn*, 693, also 816.
If people praise me,
they will also surely criticize me.
Wáng Wēng sent Commandant Mèng Sūn to Mount Tài to perform a sacrificial offering.
Passing through Xúzhōu on the way,
the Governor of Xúzhōu, Sòng Zhòngwēng,
spoke of my talent and wisdom, comparing me to Chén Píng and
the Marquis of Liú (Liú Hóu).
When Mèng Sūn returned,
he joyfully said to me:
"Zhòngwēng praised your great virtue,
is this really you?"
I replied:
"You have been traveling with me for four or five years,
yet I have never heard you praise me.
Now you hear a single word from Zhòngwēng
and are surprised by it.
If someone slanders me,
would you also believe it?
I fear you!"
See *Yì Lín*.
*Zhōu Yì* says:
"A fat retreat, nothing is unfavorable."
See the commentary to Xiè Língyù's "Entering Huázigāng Poem" in *Wén Xuǎn*.
King Kāng of Sòng made a helmet without a head guard
to show his bravery.
See *Yù Lǎn*, six hundred and eighty-four.
A biography states:
Chúnyú Kūn went to a neighbor's house
Seeing that the chimney was straight
and the firewood piled beside it,
he said,
"This is likely to have a fire disaster."
He advised them to rebuild the chimney in a curved shape
and move the firewood far away.
The owner of the stove did not listen.
Later, disaster struck,
and the fire indeed reached the firewood
and burned down his house.
The neighbors all came to the rescue,
and the fire was eventually extinguished.
Then, they prepared lamb and wine
to thank those who had helped put out the fire.
However, they certainly did not invite Chún yú Kūn 淳于髡 to drink and eat, the one who had suggested curving the chimney and moving the firewood.
A wise man ridiculed this, saying:
"Advising someone to curve the chimney and move the firewood certainly brings no favor,
but those with scorched heads and burned foreheads
are treated as honored guests."
This shows that they undervalue the fundamental
and value the superficial.
Is it only with chimneys and firewood that harm can be prevented?
People suffering from national disorder
is also the same.
Therefore, a good doctor treats illness before it develops,
and a wise ruler stops conspiracies at their source.
Later generations often err by neglecting prevention at the earliest stage
, and instead exert effort in attacking what has already become established
. Strategists are rarely rewarded
, while warriors are frequently honored.
This is like those people
who almost fail to grasp the relative importance of things.
Examining Chún yú Kūn's 淳于髡 prophecies
, one can understand everything without fail.
This is an example of perceiving subtle signs.
See *Qún Shū Zhì Yào* 群書治要.
Hàn Shēng 韓生, a doctoral student, lived in the East Temple.
For three consecutive nights, he had nightmares
, and asked people about them.
A person taught him to rise in the morning
and offer a pure prayer in the middle of the day.
On the third morning
, someone accused him of using incantations
, arrested and interrogated him
, and he died within a few days.
See *Yù Lǎn* 御覽, volume 186 and 400.
Jǐng Zǐchūn 景子春, a court attendant, was known for his divinations.
He was imprisoned for a crime.
The father of his wife, Ruò Zhū 若朱, came to the prison gate
and asked to pass on a padded jacket and trousers.
Zǐchūn 景子春 was alarmed, saying
: "Is it Zhū Jūn 朱君 who came to speak?
'Zhū 朱' is homophonous with 'zhū 誅' (to execute)
, trousers with a jacket
are cut in the middle.
I am to be executed."
Later, he was indeed executed by being cut in half at the waist.
See *Yù Lǎn* 御覽, volume 695.
